source_text: Hoc loco refellendi sunt etiam ii qui deos ex hominibus esse factos non tantum fatentur, sed ut eos laudent, etiam gloriantur, aut uirtutis gratia ut Herculem aut munerum ut Cererem ac Liberum aut artium repertarum ut Aesculapium ac Mineruam. haec uero quam inepta sint quamque non digna propter quae homines inexpiabili se scelere contaminent hostesque uero deo fiant, quo contempto mortuorum sacra suscipiunt, ex singulis rebus ostendam. uirtutem esse dicunt quae hominem tollat in caelum, non illam de qua philosophi disserunt, quae posita est in bonis animi, sed hanc corporalem quae dicitur fortitudo: quae quoniam praecipua in Hercule fuit, inmortalitatem meruisse creditur. quis tam stulte ineptus est, ut corporis uires diuinum uel etiam humanum bouum iudicet, cum sint et maiores pecudibus adtributae et uno morbo saepe frangantur uel senectute ipsa minuantur et corruant? itaque idem ille cum deformari ulceribus toros suos cerneret, nec sanari se uoluit nec senem fieri, ne quando se ipso minor aut deformior uideretur. hunc a rogo quo uiuum se ipse combusserat escendisse in caelum putauerunt eaque ipsa quae stultissime sunt admirati simulacris et imaginibus expressa et consecrata posuerunt, ut in perpetuum uanitatis illorum monumenta perstarent qui ob necem bestiarum deos fieri credidissent. sed haec fortasse Graecorum culpa sit, qui res leuissimas pro maximis semper habuerunt. quid nostri? num sapientiores? qui athleticam quidem uirtutem contemnunt, quia nihil obest, sed regiam, quia late solet nocere, sic admirantur, ut fortes ac bellicosos duces in deorum coetu locari arbitrentur; nec esse ullam aliam ad inmortalitatem uiam quam exercitus ducere, aliena uastare, delere urbes, oppida excindere, liberos populos aut trucidare aut subicere seruituti. uidelicet quo plures homines adflixerint spoliarint occiderint, eo se nobiliores et clariores putant et inanis gloriae specie capti sceleribus suis nomen uirtutis inponunt. iam mallem ut a ferarum caedibus deos sibi fingerent quam inmortalitatem tam cruentam probarent. si quis unum hominem iugulauerit, pro contaminato ac nefario habetur nec ad terrenum hoc domicilium deorum admitti eum fas putant. ille autem qui infinita hominum milia trucidarit, cruore campos inundauerit, flumina infecerit, non modo in templum, sed etiam in caelum admittitur. aput Ennium sic loquitur Africanus: 25 si fas endo plagas caelestum ascendere cuiquam est, mi soli caeli maxima porta patet, scilicet quia magnam partem generis humani extinxit ac perdidit. o in quantis tenebris, Africane, uersatus cs uel potius o poeta, qui per caedes et sanguinem patere hominibus ascensum in caelum putaueris! cui uanitati etiam Cicero adsensit. est uero inquit Africane: nam et Herculi eadem ista porta patuit; tamquam ipse plane, cum id fieret, ianitor fuerit in caelo. equidem statuere non possum dolendumne potius an ridendum putem, cum uideam graues et doctos et ut sibi uidentur sapientes uiros in tam miserandis errorum fluctibus uolutari. si haec est uirtus quae nos inmortales facit, mori equidem malim quam exitio esse quam plurimis. si aliter inmortalitas parari non potest nisi per sanguinem, quid fiet, si omnes in concordiam consenserint? quod certe fieri poterit, si pernicioso et impio furore proiecto innocentes esse ac iusti uelint. num igitur nemo erit caelo dignus? num peribit uirtus, quia hominibus in homines saeuire non dabitur? sed isti qui euersiones urbium populorumque summam gloriam conputant, otium publicum non ferent, rapient saeuient et iniuriis insolenter inlatis humanae societatis foedus inrumpent, ut habere hostem possint, quem (non) sceleratius deleant quam lacessierint. Nunc ad reliqua pergamus. nomen deorum Cereri ac Libero traditio munerum fecit. possum diuinis docere litteris uinum atque fruges ante progeniem Caeli atque Saturni fuisse in usu hominum, sed ab his sane inuenta esse fingamus. num potest plus aut maius uideri collegisse fruges iisque fractis panem facere docuisse aut uuas de uitibus lectas expressisse uinumque fecisse quam fruges ipsas aut uites generasse ac protulisse de terra? reliquerit haec sane deus humanis ingeniis eruenda, tamen fieri non potest quin ipsius sint omnia, qui et sapientiam tribuit homini ut inueniret et illa ipsa quae possent inueniri. artes quoque inuentoribus suis inmortalitatem peperisse dicuntur, ut Aesculapio medicina, Volcano fabrica. colamus igitur et illos qui fullonicam sutrinamue docuerunt. cur autem figulinae repertori honos non habetur? an quia isti diuites uasa Samia contemnunt? sunt et aliae artes quarum repertores humanae uitae plurimum profuerunt: cur non et illis adtributa sunt templa? sed nimirum Minerua est quae omnes repperit, ideoque illi opifices supplicant. ergo ab his sordibus Minerua ascendit in caelum. est uero cur quisquam derelinquat eum qui terram cum animantibus, caelum cum astris et luminibus exorsus est, ut eam ueneretur quae telam docuit ordiri. quid ille qui uulnera in corporibus sanare docuit? num potest esse praestantior quam qui corpora ipsa formauit, sentiendi ac uiuendi rationem dedit, herbas denique ipsas et cetera quibus medendi ars constat excogitauit ac protulit?
pass_a_gloss: In this place, those who confess that gods were made from men, not only acknowledge this, but also boast about it, in order to praise them, either on account of virtue, as in the case of Hercules, or on account of gifts, as in the case of Ceres and Liber, or on account of the discovery of arts, as in the case of Aesculapius and Minerva. But these things are truly foolish and unworthy, for which men pollute themselves with inexpiable crime and become enemies of God, despising the dead, and receiving sacred rites. I will show from individual things. They say that virtue is what lifts a man to heaven, not that virtue which philosophers discuss, which is situated in the goods of the soul, but this bodily virtue which is called strength. Since this was preeminent in Hercules, he is believed to have deserved immortality. Who is so foolish and inept that he judges divine or even human good by the strength of the body, when these are also attributed to beasts and are often broken by one disease or diminished and corrupted by old age itself? Therefore, the same Hercules, when he saw his bed being deformed by ulcers, did not want to be healed nor to become old, lest he seem lesser or more deformed to himself. They thought that he ascended to heaven from the pyre on which he had burned himself alive, and they admired and consecrated the very things that are most foolish, expressed in statues and images, so that the monuments of their vanity might persist forever, who believed that gods were made on account of the death of beasts. But perhaps this is the fault of the Greeks, who always considered the most trivial things as the greatest. What about our own people? Are they any wiser? Who contemptuously reject athletic virtue, because it is of no use, but admire royal virtue, because it often does harm, so that they think that brave and warlike leaders are placed among the gods; and they think that there is no other way to immortality than to lead armies, to devastate foreign lands, to destroy cities, to cut down towns, to slaughter or enslave free peoples. Obviously, the more men they have afflicted, plundered, and killed, the more noble and famous they think themselves, and, captivated by the appearance of empty glory, they impose the name of virtue on their crimes. I would rather that they fabricated gods from the slaughter of beasts than proved such a bloody immortality. If someone has killed one man, he is considered contaminated and nefarious, and it is not right to admit him to this earthly dwelling of the gods. But he who has slaughtered countless thousands of men, has flooded the fields with blood, and polluted the rivers, is not only admitted to the temple, but also to heaven. Africanus says in Ennius: If it is right for anyone to ascend to the heavenly regions, the greatest gate of heaven is open to me alone, obviously because I have extinguished and destroyed a great part of the human race. Oh, in what great darkness, Africanus, you have been, or rather, oh poet, who thinks that the ascent to heaven is open to men through slaughter and bloodshed! Cicero also assented to this vanity. For Africanus says: For the same gate was open to Hercules; as if he himself were clearly the doorkeeper in heaven when this happened. I am unable to determine whether it is more to be lamented or ridiculed, when I see grave and learned men, and those who seem wise to themselves, being tossed about in such miserable waves of error. If this is the virtue that makes us immortal, I would rather die than be the cause of destruction for many. If immortality cannot be obtained in any other way than through bloodshed, what will happen if all men agree to live in harmony? Which can certainly happen, if they reject pernicious and impious fury and want to be innocent and just. Will no one then be worthy of heaven? Will virtue perish, because men will not be allowed to rage against each other? But those who consider the destruction of cities and peoples as the greatest glory, will not tolerate public peace, will seize and rage, and will insolently inflict injuries, breaking the pact of human society, so that they may have an enemy to destroy, whom they may slay more wickedly than they provoked. Now let us proceed to the rest. The tradition of gifts has given the name of gods to Ceres and Liber. I can teach from divine writings that wine and grain were in use among men before the progeny of Caelus and Saturnus, but let us suppose that they were discovered by them. Can it seem greater or more remarkable to have collected grain and to have taught men to make bread from it, or to have gathered grapes from vines and to have made wine, than to have generated grain itself or vines and to have brought them forth from the earth? Although God may have left these things to be discovered by human ingenuity, nevertheless, it cannot be that they are not His, who has given wisdom to men to discover them, and those very things that can be discovered. The arts are also said to have conferred immortality on their discoverers, as medicine on Aesculapius, and craftsmanship on Vulcan. Let us therefore also honor those who have taught fulling or shoemaking. Why does the discoverer of pottery not receive honor? Is it because the rich despise Samian vessels? There are also other arts whose discoverers have greatly benefited human life: why have temples not been dedicated to them? But perhaps Minerva is the one who has discovered all things, and therefore the craftsmen pray to her. Therefore, Minerva ascends to heaven from these vile things. Is it really the case that someone would abandon Him who created the earth with living creatures, the heaven with stars and lights, in order to venerate her who taught how to weave a web? What about him who taught how to heal wounds on bodies? Can he be more excellent than He who formed the bodies themselves, gave the reason for feeling and living, and finally devised and brought forth the herbs and other things by which the art of healing consists?
pass_b_english: Here I must also refute those who not only confess that gods originated from human beings, but actually boast of it in order to honor them—whether for their virtue, as with Hercules, for their gifts, as with Ceres and Liber, or for their discovery of arts, as with Aesculapius and Minerva. Such claims are utterly foolish and unworthy; they lead people to defile themselves with inexpiable guilt and make themselves enemies of God, since they despise the true God while devoting sacred rites to the dead. I will demonstrate the falsity of each point in turn. They claim that the virtue which elevates a human to heaven is not the moral excellence that philosophers discuss—the kind rooted in the goods of the soul—but merely physical strength. Because this bodily prowess was preeminent in Hercules, he is said to have earned immortality. Who could be so foolish as to judge divine or even human worth by bodily strength, when beasts possess it in greater measure, and a single illness or old age itself can break or diminish it? Hence, when Hercules saw his own flesh deformed by ulcers, he refused both healing and the prospect of growing old, lest he ever appear lesser or more deformed to himself. People imagined that he ascended to heaven from the pyre on which he burned himself alive, and they revered and consecrated the very things that are most absurd, preserving them in statues and images so that monuments to their vanity would endure forever—all because they believed gods could be made through the killing of beasts. Perhaps this is a Greek failing, since they have always treated the most trivial things as the greatest. But what of our own people? Are they any wiser? They scorn athletic virtue because it serves no practical purpose, yet they admire royal virtue precisely because it tends to cause widespread harm. Consequently, they assume that brave and warlike commanders gain a place among the gods, and they insist that the only road to immortality is to lead armies, ravage foreign lands, demolish cities, raze towns, and either slaughter or enslave free peoples. Clearly, the more men they afflict, plunder, and kill, the more noble and renowned they consider themselves; seduced by the illusion of empty glory, they attach the name of virtue to their own crimes. I would rather they invented gods from the slaughter of beasts than validate an immortality so drenched in blood. If someone kills a single human being, he is regarded as polluted and accursed, and it is deemed unlawful to admit him into this earthly dwelling of the gods. Yet the one who has slaughtered countless thousands, flooded fields with blood, and poisoned rivers is welcomed not only into the temple but into heaven itself. In Ennius, Africanus declares: "If it is permitted for anyone to ascend to the heavenly realms, the widest gate of heaven stands open to me alone" —precisely because he has wiped out and destroyed a great portion of the human race. Oh, what profound darkness you dwell in, Africanus—or rather, oh poet, who imagined that the ascent to heaven lies open to mortals through slaughter and bloodshed! Even Cicero gave his assent to this vanity. "It is true," he says, "Africanus; for that same gate was open to Hercules" —as if he himself had been the doorkeeper of heaven when it happened. I cannot decide whether to weep or laugh when I see serious, learned men, who regard themselves as wise, tossed about in such wretched waves of error. If this is the virtue that makes us immortal, I would rather die than become the cause of destruction for countless people. If immortality can be obtained only through bloodshed, what happens when all humanity agrees to live in harmony—something that can certainly occur if people renounce their ruinous and impious fury and choose to be innocent and just? Will no one then be worthy of heaven? Will virtue perish simply because men are no longer allowed to rage against one another? But those who count the overthrow of cities and peoples as the highest glory will never tolerate public peace; they will seize, rampage, and insolently inflict injuries, shattering the covenant of human society just so they can have an enemy to destroy more wickedly than they provoked. Now let us proceed to the remaining cases. Tradition assigned the title of gods to Ceres and Liber because of their gifts. I could prove from divine writings that grain and wine were already in human use before the offspring of Caelus and Saturn appeared, but let us suppose for argument's sake that these two discovered them. Can gathering grain and teaching people to bake bread from it, or pressing grapes from vines and making wine, really appear greater or more remarkable than creating the grain and the vines themselves and bringing them forth from the earth? Even if God left such discoveries to human ingenuity, it remains impossible that they are not His, since He gave human beings the wisdom to discover them and brought the discoverable things into existence. The arts, too, are said to have conferred immortality on their discoverers—medicine on Aesculapius, metalworking on Vulcan. Then let us also honor those who taught fulling or shoemaking. Why does the inventor of pottery receive no honor? Is it because the rich despise Samian ware? There are other arts whose discoverers have enormously benefited human life; why have temples not been dedicated to them as well? But perhaps Minerva is credited with discovering everything, and so craftsmen pray to her. Thus Minerva ascends to heaven from these lowly origins. Is it really plausible that anyone would abandon the One who created the earth with its living creatures and the heavens with their stars and lights, in order to venerate the one who merely taught how to weave a web? And what of the one who taught how to heal bodily wounds? Can he be more excellent than the One who formed the bodies themselves, gave them the capacity to feel and live, and originally devised and brought forth the herbs and all the other substances on which the art of healing depends?

review.notes: The translation accurately reflects the Latin text, preserving the nuances of agency (e.g., 'who has given wisdom' vs 'who has given human beings wisdom'), modality, and the author's rhetorical structure. Scripture/Classical citations (Ennius/Africanus and Cicero) are correctly integrated and attributed. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source.
